parts.description: A white glazed ceramic colander with a deep perforated bowl, rounded rim, loop side handles, and a raised foot ring. The surface is smooth and glossy with regularly spaced drainage holes through the lower bowl.
parts.reasoning: The object appears to be a medium household ceramic colander, roughly 0.24–0.28 m in bowl diameter, about 0.14–0.17 m tall, and about 0.32–0.36 m wide including the handles. Glazed stoneware/porcelain has a true material density around 2200–2500 kg/m^3; 2300 kg/m^3 is used as the dominant material density. Because the object is a hollow thin-walled shell with holes, handles, rim thickening, and a pedestal foot, the total solid ceramic volume is much smaller than its bounding volume. Assuming a 5–7 mm wall thickness, reinforced rim and base, and material removed by perforations, a realistic mass is about 1.25 kg. The center of mass should lie on the vertical symmetry axis, slightly below the geometric mid-height because of the thicker foot ring and lower bowl mass. The dominant contact material is smooth glazed ceramic, but the bottom foot ring may be slightly less polished; static friction is estimated at 0.50 and dynamic friction at 0.38 for dry contact against common work surfaces. Restitution is set to 0.42: ceramic is hard and can rebound from rigid surfaces, but a hollow bowl dissipates energy through vibration and impacts should not be made overly bouncy. For collision, a single convex hull would incorrectly close the open bowl and ignore the concavity and handles. An SDF mesh is the most faithful option for the open concave bowl and drainage perforations; for higher-performance scenes, a simplified convex decomposition should be substituted if the holes do not need to participate in contact. Hard-body contact offsets are kept small, with 0.0 m rest offset and about 0.004 m contact offset, to avoid visible hovering while still generating stable contacts around the thin rim and foot. CCD is recommended because the model has thin ceramic walls and small perforation features that can tunnel during drops or fast robot interactions. Compliant contacts are disabled by default because this is a rigid ceramic object; if contact chatter occurs, use very stiff, lightly damped compliance rather than soft material behavior.
